meta.title: All Roads Lead to Palmer — Supervisor Oversight of Misconduct

narrative.summary: All named officers in Ben Carter’s case (Dixon, Clarke, Gasson, Russell, Butcher, Duffy) operated under the oversight of Inspector David Palmer. This places Palmer as the supervisory anchor for systemic failures, contradictions, and unlawful data handling across Sussex Police’s treatment of Carter. Each officer had an individual duty to act under the Code of Ethics, but collectively their misconduct occurred within Palmer’s chain of command, making him directly responsible for oversight failures and complicit through inaction.
context: PC Jon Dixon: declared NFA, issued harassment threats, denied safeguarding.
PC Clarke: fabricated welfare contacts, ignored lawful challenges.
PC Gasson: introduced as 'new OIC' after NFA, welfare messages misrepresented.
PC Russell / DC Mark Butcher: repeatedly named in communications, blocked evidence submission.
Sergeant Duffy: escalated but no safeguarding action taken.
All these officers were under the line management and oversight of Inspector David Palmer.
contradiction_points: Sussex Police cannot claim misconduct was isolated when all named officers were under Palmer’s watch.
Palmer received correspondence and was directly aware of systemic failures yet took no corrective action.
Supervisory duty requires intervention where safeguarding and honesty are breached — silence = complicity.
Misconduct cascaded down the chain of command, with Palmer as the accountable supervisory node.
legal_analysis: College of Policing Code of Ethics — supervisors must uphold accountability, honesty, integrity.
Police Reform Act 2002 — duty to handle complaints and misconduct transparently.
Human Rights Act 1998, Articles 2, 3, 8 — duty to protect life, dignity, and prevent degrading treatment.
Common Law: Misconduct in Public Office — knowing silence and inaction in the face of wrongdoing.
narrative.emotional_impact: For the victim, every officer deflection, fabrication, or silence was compounded by the knowledge that an Inspector was copied into correspondence and failed to act. This demonstrated institutional betrayal at supervisory level, escalating harm and cementing the collapse of trust.
